Acted with generous doses of stage-filling warmth by a terrific cast, the play is acutely well-observed, sexually frank and often funny, even if, as it meanders toward three hours, you might begin to wonder whether all its events are worth such extended attention.
The production elements come together seamlessly on the larger stage at TFANA.
But, if Public Obscenities never bores, it also never fully engages.
While Public Obscenities ambles along, the drama is decidedly rewarding but sometimes so relaxed it all but becomes lackadaisical.
A wonderful production with a strong cast and fabulous design, Public Obscenities left me wanting more...

Public Obscenities manages to maintain interest in an overlong, overwritten play that often seems about little more than the trivialities of human interaction, paying lip service to potentially significant matters that drift off into obscurity.
However, it can be difficult for audiences to fully understand everything at times since parts of the dialogue in Bangla are missing English subtitles.
Shayok Misha Chowdhury’s bilingual Public Obscenities is the surprise hit of the season.

cn.t: Critics praise Shayok Misha Chowdhury's bilingual debut as exquisitely crafted and culturally rich, celebrating its warm performances, evocative production design, and frank exploration of queer life in Kolkata.
